reenactor.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English enact English reenact English -or English reenactor From reenact + -or.

d.g: information that makes more forcible or convincing
The condition of being reenlisted
d.x: Despite consistently high evaluations from supervisors, Watkins was denied reenlistment because he said he was gay.

d.g: A second or subsequent enlistment

reenlistment.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English enlistment English reenlistment From re- + enlistment.

d.g: Alternative form of re-entry.
A second or subsequent evaluation or rating

reevaluation.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English evaluation English reevaluation From re- + evaluation.

d.g: Any of several local officials, with varying responsibilities.
d.x: His first convert was the reeve of the city of Lincoln called Blæcca, ...

d.g: The president of a township or municipal district council.
The holder of a proposed but unadopted commissioned rank of the Royal Air Force, equivalent to wing commander.
To pass (a rope) through a hole or opening, especially so as to fasten it.
d.x: "Let the rope go," he says. With his other hand he reaches down and reeves the two turns from the stanchion.

reeve.e: From Middle English reve, from Old English rēfa, an aphetism of ġerēfa (also grœ̄fa), from Proto-West Germanic *garāfijō (“officer, official”). Compare Danish greve, Swedish greve, Dutch graaf, German Graf. The role, and eventually the word, was mostly replaced by bailiff, of Anglo-Norman origin.

d.g: Alternative form of re-examination.
Clipping of referee.
Abbreviation of reference.
Clipping of refsheet.
Abbreviation of refectory.
Fabrication again or anew; remanufacture.
Mental or spiritual refreshment.
Physical refreshment, especially with food or drink.
A meal, especially a light meal.

refection.e: From French réfection, from Latin refectiōnem, accusative singular of refectiō (“recovery, refection”), from reficiō (“restore, renew”).

d.g: A dining hall, especially in an institution such as a college or monastery.
d.x: They compare very well with similar cafes elsewhere and the quality, for example, is far better and the price cheaper than in my college refectory.

refectory.e: Via Middle English refectori from Late Latin refectorium, from Latin reficere (“to remake, to rebuild”).

d.g: An umpire or judge; an official who makes sure the rules are followed during a game.
d.x: The referee kicked Jim out of the game for fighting.

d.g: A person who settles a dispute.
A person who writes a letter of reference or provides a reference by phone call for someone. (In the UK such a person is sometimes, and in the US the person is typically, referred to as a reference.)
d.x: Your application, along with letters from three referees, should be received by January 31.

d.g: An expert who judges the manuscript of an article or book to decide if it should be published.

referee.e: From Middle English [Term?], from past participle of Old French referer (“to relate, to refer”), from Latin referre (“to carry back, to report, to notify”); as if refer + -ee, that is, the person to whom something is referred for consideration.

d.g: present participle and gerund of referee
The act by which something is refereed.
The peer review process.
A measurement one can compare (some other measurement) to.
Information about a person, provided by someone (a referee) with whom they are well acquainted.
A person who provides this information; a referee.
A reference work.
d.x: reference grammar

reference.e: From Middle French référence, from Medieval Latin referentia, nominative neuter plural of referēns, present participle of referō (“return, reply”, literally “carry back”). Morphologically refer + -ence.

d.g: A direct popular vote on a proposed law or constitutional amendment.
d.x: a referendum on …

d.g: An action, choice, etc., which is perceived as passing judgment on another matter.
d.x: My father is taking my decision on whether to go to university as a referendum on his performance as a parent, and it's very stressful.

referendum.e: From Latin referendum (“that which ought to be announced”), from refero (“to announce”).

d.g: The act or process of transferring someone or something to another, of sending by reference, or referring.
d.x: The insurance company insists I get a referral from my regular doctor. I can't just go to the specialist; a GP has got to refer me.

d.g: A document used by schools detailing some form of a student's misbehavior and listing the actions taken before and after the student's receipt of the referral.
d.x: After misbehaving in class, George was given a referral for disrupting class and sent to the office.

referral.e: English refer Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-der.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English referral From refer + -al.

d.g: An additional helping of food or drink at reduced cost.
d.x: Today it is $2 for a coffee, with free refills throughout the day.

d.g: Refuelling, fuel to refill an empty fuel tank (of a vehicle or machine) or other fuel container.
d.x: Tank's empty. We need to go for a refill.

d.g: A product intended to replace the used contents of a container or the exhausted supply of a device.
d.x: We're cutting back. No new printers or pens, just refills.

d.g: A repeat of a prescription.

refill.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English fill English refill From re- (“again”) + fill (noun).

d.g: present participle and gerund of refill
The act of filling again; a refill.
The act, or the result of refining; the removal of impurities, or a purified material
High-class style; cultivation.
A fine or subtle distinction.
A luxury.
d.x: There was no bathroom in the cabin. Such refinements don't exist in the woods, apparently.

refinement.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English fine English refine Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English refinement From refine + -ment.

d.g: One who, or that which, refines.
d.x: The average motorist will not see much, if any, difference in gasoline pump price but oil producers and Gulf Coast refiners expect profits to improve.

refiner.e: English refine Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English refiner From refine + -er.

d.g: A building, or a mass of machinery, used to produce refined products such as sugar, oil, or metals.
d.x: Pipeable products may be moved from refinery centers to demand zones by truck, barge, intercoastal tanker or pipeline.

refinery.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English fine English refine Middle English -re,-ri,-rie,-ry,-rye English -ry English refinery From refine + -ry.

d.g: present participle and gerund of refine
Refinement (process of refining)
A provider of refinishing services
d.x: In addition to referring customers to local refinishers, Mr. Rountree’s company also sells refinishing products to do-it-yourselfers.

refinisher.e: English refinish English -er English refinisher From refinish + -er.

d.g: The process of having something fitted again, repaired or restored.
d.x: The ship required a refit before setting out again.

d.g: To fit again; to put back into its place.
d.x: Michelangelo took a group outside and in full view of the papal troops refitted the fallen, shattered stone into the walls.

d.g: To prepare for use again; to repair or restore.
d.x: to refit a garment; to refit ships of war

d.g: To fit out or supply again (with something).

refit.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English fit English refit From re- + fit.

d.g: The act of restoring a deflated general level of prices to a previous or desired level.
d.x: This continues until there is a reflation, a currency devaluation and government guarantees of the efficacy of key financial intermediaries.

d.g: The ratio of the flux reflected to that incident on a surface.

reflectance.e: English reflect Proto-Indo-European *-yós Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -iader. Old French -ancebor. Middle English -aunce English -ance English reflectance From reflect + -ance.

d.g: The act of reflecting or the state of being reflected.
The property of a propagated wave being thrown back from a surface (such as a mirror).
Something, such as an image, that is reflected.
d.x: The dog barked at his own reflection in the mirror.

d.g: Careful thought or consideration.
d.x: After careful reflection, I have decided not to vote for that proposition.

reflection.e: From Middle English refleccion, refleccioun, refleccioune, reflection, from Middle French reflection, reflexion, and its source Late Latin reflexiō, from the participle stem of reflectō. The current spelling is influenced by reflect. Equivalent to reflect + -ion.

d.g: The state or property of being reflective.

reflectiveness.e: English reflective Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English reflectiveness From reflective + -ness.

d.g: The property or quality of being reflective.

reflectivity.e: English reflect Proto-Indo-European *-wós Proto-Indo-European *-iHwósder. Latin -īvus Old French -ifbor. Middle English -yf English -ive English reflective Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Latin -itāsder. Old French -itebor. …

d.g: An instrument used to measure the reflectance of a surface.

reflectometer.e: English reflect Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. English -o- Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-tḗr Proto-Indo-European *-trom Proto-Hellenic *-tron Ancient Greek -τρον (-tron) Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron)der. English -meter English reflectometer From reflect + -o- + -meter.

d.g: Something which reflects heat, light or sound, especially something having a reflecting surface.
A reflecting telescope.
A small, often red, reflecting disk on the rear of a vehicle or bicycle that reflects the headlights of other vehicles.
A safety reflector.

reflector.e: English reflect English -or English reflector From reflect + -or.

d.g: Dated spelling of reflection.
d.x: He gets off the train, determined not to leave town after all. But a little further reflexion shows him the folly of such a course.

d.g: An act or instance of referring back to the subject of a sentence, or of having an object equal to the subject.

reflexion.e: From Middle English reflexion, reflexioun, from Middle French reflexion and its etymon Late Latin reflexiō; the variant spelling reflection is due to influence from correction.

d.g: The state or quality of being reflexive.
The condition or state of being reflexive.

reflexivity.e: English reflexive Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Latin -itāsder. Old French -itebor. Middle English -ite English -ity English reflexivity From reflexive + -ity.

d.g: The study and interpretation of behavior in terms of simple and complex reflexes.

A form of complementary medicine involving the stimulation of points on the feet, hands, or ears, in the belief that it will have a beneficial effect on some other parts of the body or to improve general health.
The backwards flow of any fluid.
A technique, using a reflux condenser, allowing one to boil the contents of a vessel over an extended period.
The leaking of stomach acid up into the oesophagus.
To flow back or return.
d.x: the refluxing tide

d.g: present participle and gerund of refocus
A change of focus.
The act or process of replanting a forest, especially after clear-cutting.

reforestation.e: English reforest Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor. Middle English -acioun English -ation English reforestation From reforest + -ation.

d.g: The change of something that is defective, broken, inefficient or otherwise negative, in order to correct or improve it
d.x: The elections need to undergo a serious reform.

d.g: To put into a new and improved form or condition; to restore to a former good state, or bring from bad to good; to change from worse to better.
d.x: to reform a profligate man; to reform corrupt manners or morals; to reform a criminal

d.g: To return to a good state; to amend or correct one's own character or habits.
d.x: It is hoped that many criminals, upon being freed, will eventually reform.

d.g: To form again or in a new configuration.
d.x: This product contains reformed meat.

reform.e: From Middle English reformen, from Old French reformer, from Latin reformo, reformare. As a noun since 1660s, from French réforme.

d.g: An improvement (or an intended improvement) in the existing form or condition of institutions or practices, etc.; intended to make a striking change for the better in social, political or religious affairs or in the conduct of persons or operation of organizations.
d.x: […] olde men long nusled in corruption, scorning them that would seeke reformation […]

d.g: Change or correction, by a court in equity, to a written instrument to conform to the original intention of the parties.
Alternative form of re-formation.

reformation.e: From Middle English reformacioun, reformation, from Middle French reformation and Latin refōrmātiō, refōrmātiōnis (“reform, change”), from refōrmō (“transform, reshape”), from re- + fōrmō (“shape, form”). By surface analysis, reform + -ation.

d.g: One who reforms, or who works for reform.
One who was involved in the Reformation.
d.x: […] for I long to ſee a larke without a creaſt, and would travaile farre to diſcoover a reformer without a fault, […]

d.g: A device which converts hydrocarbons into a hydrogen-rich mixture of gases.
A device used to convert petroleum refinery naphthas, typically having low octane ratings, into high-octane liquid products called reformates.

reformer.e: English reform Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English reformer From reform + -er.

d.g: Any of several movements that promote reform

reformism.e: English reform Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English reformism From reform + -ism.

d.g: The turning or bending of any wave, such as a light or sound wave, when it passes from one medium into another of different optical density.
The degree to which a metal or compound can withstand heat

refraction.e: Latin refringō Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin refrāctiōbor. English refraction Borrowed from Latin refrāctiō.

d.g: The quality or condition of being refractive.
The quality or degree of being refractive.
An optical instrument used to measure the refractive index of a substance.

refractometer.e: English refract Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. English -o- Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-tḗr Proto-Indo-European *-trom Proto-Hellenic *-tron Ancient Greek -τρον (-tron) Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron)der. English -meter English refractometer From refract + -o- + -meter.

d.g: The quality of being refractory.

refractoriness.e: English refractory Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English refractoriness From refractory + -ness.

d.g: To stop oneself from some action or interference; to abstain; to eschew
d.x: Refrain from these men, and let them alone.

d.g: To abstain from (food or drink).
d.x: Who, requiring a remedy for his gout, received no other counsel than to refrain cold drink.

d.g: The chorus or burden of a song repeated at the end of each verse or stanza.
A much repeated comment, complaint, or saying.

refrain.e: Inherited from Middle English refreynen, from Anglo-Norman refrener, Old French refrener, from Latin refrēnāre, from re- + frēnāre, from frēnum.

d.g: Something that refreshes.
d.x: The nap was a welcome refresher.

d.g: A review to refresh or renew knowledge.
d.x: They recommend a refresher class every few years.

d.g: A fee paid to counsel to continue with a case, especially one that was adjourned.
An equity grant given by a company to an existing employee, as opposed to an initial grant given to new employees.

refresher.e: English refresh Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English refresher From refresh + -er.

d.g: The process of refreshing; a means of restoring strength, energy or vigour.
That which refreshes, such as a light snack or drink.
d.x: All refreshments will be provided by the hosts.

d.g: The result of being refreshed.

refreshment.e: Recorded since 1665; either directly or via Middle English refreschement, from Old French refrescher (12th century; modern French rafraîchir), itself from re- (“again”) + fresche (“fresh”) (modern French frais; from a Germanic source, cognate with Old High German frisc, modern German frisch, Dutch fris, etc.)

d.g: The process of transferring heat from an object in order to cool it.
The process of preserving something by cooling.
The cooling of the body for therapeutic purposes.
A household or commercial appliance used for keeping food fresh by refrigeration (short form fridge).
d.x: Meronym: condenser

d.g: A similar device used to keep non-food items cold, such as blood, photographic film, drugs, or pharmaceuticals like insulin.
d.x: Meronym: condenser

d.g: One who has a chilling influence.
d.x: […] in a state of sublime satisfaction, he moves among the company, a magnificent refrigerator.

d.g: present participle and gerund of refuel
The act of providing or taking on more fuel
A state of safety, protection or shelter.
d.x: Rocks, dens, and caves! But I in none of these / Find place or refuge.

d.g: A place providing safety, protection or shelter.
Something or someone turned to for safety or assistance; a recourse or resort.
d.x: Since its conception, the European Union has been a haven for those seeking refuge from war, persecution and poverty in other parts of the world.

d.g: An expedient to secure protection or defence.
d.x: Their latest refuge / Was to send him.

refuge.e: From Middle English refuge, from Old French refuge, from Latin refugium, from re- + fugiō (“flee”). Doublet of refugium.

d.g: A person seeking refuge (as for shelter or protection), especially in a foreign country, out of fear or prospect of political, religious persecution, war, natural disaster, etc.
d.x: In 1962 a special law had to be passed to permit the immigration of several thousand Chinese refugees who had escaped from Communist China to Hong Kong.

d.g: A person who is fleeing from justice, punishment deemed righteous, etc.; a runaway, a fugitive.
To convey (slaves) away from the advance of the federal forces.

refugee.e: From French réfugié, past participle of réfugier (“to take refuge, to seek refuge”), from Old French refuge (“hiding place”) from Latin refugium (“a place of refuge, place to flee back to”), originally describing French Huguenots fleeing religious persecution after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685. …

d.g: the quality of being refulgent; refulgency
d.x: In a parallel way the refulgence of Jesus's body at the Transfiguration was miraculous, transitory, like sun lighting up the air.

refulgence.e: From Latin refulgentia. By surface analysis, re- + Latin fulg(ere) + -ence.

d.g: The property of being refulgent.

refulgency.e: By surface analysis, re- + Latin fulg(ere) + -ency.

d.g: To return (money) to (someone); to reimburse.
d.x: If you find this computer for sale anywhere at a lower price, we’ll refund you the difference.

d.g: To obtain a refund.
d.x: This game sucks, Imma refund it.

d.g: An amount of money returned.
d.x: If the camera is faulty, you can return it to the store where you bought it for a full refund.

refund.e: From Middle English refunden, refounden, from Old French refondre, refonder, refunder (“to restore; pay back”), from Latin refundere; prefix re- (“re-”) + fundere (“to pour”): compare French refondre, refonder. See fuse (“to melt”), and compare refound (“to cast again”), and refuse.

d.g: The act of refurbishing; a renovation.

refurbishment.e: English refurbish Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English refurbishment From refurbish + -ment.

d.g: The act of refusing.
d.x: Your refusal to carry out your duties resulted in your sacking.

d.g: Depth or point at which well or borehole drilling cannot continue.

refusal.e: From Middle English refusell; equivalent to refuse + -al.

d.g: Discarded, rejected.
Collectively, items or material that have been discarded; rubbish, garbage.
To decline (a request or demand).
d.x: My request for a pay rise was refused.

d.g: To decline a request or demand, forbear; to withhold permission.
d.x: I refuse to listen to this nonsense any more.

refuse.e: Borrowed into late Middle English from Middle French refusé, past participle of refuser (“to refuse”). Displaced native Middle English wernen (“to refuse”) likely due to the similar sounding Middle English warnen

d.g: Synonym of refutation.

refutal.e: English refute Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English refutal From refute + -al.

d.g: An act of refuting or disproving; the disproving of an argument, opinion, testimony, doctrine or theory by argument or countervailing proof; evidence of falseness.
d.x: Near-synonyms: rebuttal (see note), counterargument, counterassertion, counterclaim, denial

d.g: A vocal answer to an attack on one's assertions.

refutation.e: Borrowed from Middle French refutation (compare French réfutation, Spanish refutación, Portuguese refutação, Italian refutazione) or its etymon Latin refūtātiō, from refūtō + -ātiō. By surface analysis, refute + -ation. First attested in 1536 (in sense 1).

d.g: A person who refutes with an argument or example.
An argument or example that refutes.

refuter.e: English refute English -er English refuter From refute + -er.

d.g: present participle and gerund of regain
The act by which something is regained.
ribbonfishes
Royal rights, prerogatives and privileges actually enjoyed by any sovereign, regardless of his title (emperor, grand duke etc.).
The emblems, symbols, or paraphernalia indicative of royalty or any other sovereign status; such as a crown, orb, sceptre or sword.
Decorations or insignia indicative of an office or membership of an order or society; such as freemasonry.
Traditional dress and accessories of North American Indigenous nations worn for ritual purposes.

regalia.e: From Middle English regalie, from Medieval Latin rēgālia (“royal powers”), substantivisation of the neuter plural of rēgālis (“of a king”), from rēx (“king”). By surface analysis, regal + -ia.

d.g: A steady look, a gaze.
One's concern for another; esteem; relation, reference.
A particular aspect or detail; respect, sense.
d.x: This attempt will be made with every regard to the difficulty of the undertaking […]

d.g: The worth or estimation in which something or someone is held.
d.x: He is held in great regard in Whitehall.

regard.e: From Middle English regard, regarde, reguard, from Anglo-Norman reguard, from regarder, reguarder. Attested in Middle English starting around the mid 14th century. Piecewise doublet of reward; compare also guard, ward, guardian, and so on.

d.g: A series of boat races, or sometimes a single race.
d.x: […] many people living along the harbour front had boathouses and boats of their own, for regattas and water sports were one of Victoria's chief attractions.

d.g: A striped cotton fabric.

regatta.e: From Italian (Venetian dialect) regatta (“contention for mastery”), from regattare (“compete, haggle, sell at retail”), possibly from ricattare; or from Italian regata (“boat race, regatta”), via Vulgar Latin *aurigata from Latin auriga.

d.g: A system of government that substitutes for the reign of a king or queen when that king or queen becomes unable to rule.
The time during which a regent is in power.
An administrative division ranking below a province in Indonesia.

regency.e: From Middle English regencie (cf. regente), from Medieval Latin regentia, from Latin regēns, present participle of regō. By surface analysis, regent + -cy; compare also + -ency (“abstract-noun suffix”).

d.g: Rebuilding or restructuring; large scale repair or renewal; revitalisation.
d.x: The conversion of so many old industrial buildings into living quarters was a major factor in the regeneration.

d.g: Spiritual rebirth; the change from a carnal or material life to a pious one
The renewal of the world at the second coming of Christ.
The process by which a water softener flushes out minerals extracted from the water supply.

regeneration.e: From re- + generation or regenerate + -ion, from Latin regenerātiō.

d.g: A music genre that originated in Jamaica in the late 1960s and is heavily associated with Rastafarianism, featuring a heavy bass line and percussive rhythm guitar on the offbeat, often with close vocal harmonies.
d.x: Near-synonym: (earlier) bluebeat

reggae.e: From Jamaican Creole rege (“rags; a quarrel”), see rag; originally used in the 1960s to describe a Jamaican dance. Compare ragtime. Broader musical sense popularized by the 1968 Maytals song “Do the Reggay”.

d.g: a town in central Algeria
The killing of a king.
One who kills a king.

regicide.e: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rēgicidium (“king-killing”)

d.g: Mode of rule or management.
d.x: a prison regime

d.g: A form of government, or the government in power, particularly an authoritarian or totalitarian one.
d.x: the dictator's regime

d.g: A period of rule.
A regulated system; a regimen.
d.x: a fitness regime

regime.e: From Middle English regime, regyme, from Middle French regime, from Latin regimen (“direction, government”). Doublet of regimen.

d.g: Orderly government; system of order; administration.
d.x: In ski areas like Arapahoe Basin, about 80 percent of the male patrollers have had to drastically change (or introduce) shaving regimens.

d.g: Any regulation or remedy which is intended to produce beneficial effects by gradual operation.
d.x: Seven or eight annual bloodings, and as many purgations — such was the common regimen the theory prescribed to ensure continuance of health[…]

d.g: Object.
d.x: Pronouns may be nominatives, and of the direct or indirect regimen.

d.g: A syntactical relation between words, as when one depends on another and is regulated by it in respect to case or mood; government.

regimen.e: From Middle English regimen, from Middle French regimen and its etymon, Latin regimen (“guidance, direction, government, rule”). Doublet of regime.

d.g: A unit of armed troops under the command of an officer, and consisting of several smaller units.
d.x: It was an old, withered man, who had served the Government in the days of the Mutiny as a native officer in a newly raised cavalry regiment.

d.x: Firefighters remained at the scene all day to prevent the smoldering remains from re-igniting.

d.g: To start again, especially animosity or argument.
d.x: The verdict against Yingluck is widely seen as having the potential to reignite tensions, though the junta has largely snuffed out open opposition.

reignite.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English ignite English reignite From re- + ignite.

d.g: To compensate (someone) with payment; especially, to repay money spent on someone's behalf.
d.x: The company will reimburse you for your expenses for the business trip.

d.g: To recoup (funds spent).

reimburse.e: 1591, re- (“back”) + imburse (“pay”, literally “put in a purse”) (perhaps after Middle French rembourser or Italian rimborsàre), from Middle French embourser, from Old French en- (“in”) + borser (“to get money”), from borse (“purse”), from Medieval Latin bursa (English purse).

d.g: To impose again, a further time.

reimpose.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English impose English reimpose From re- + impose.

d.g: To strengthen, especially by addition or augmentation.
d.x: He reinforced the handle with a metal rod and a bit of tape.

d.g: To emphasize or review.
d.x: The right homework will reinforce and complement the lesson!

d.g: To encourage (a behavior or idea) through repeated stimulus.
d.x: Advertising for fast food can reinforce unhealthy dietary tendencies.

reinforce.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English inforce English reinforce From re- + inforce.

d.g: To install again.
reinstallation
d.x: I tried removing and reinstalling the software, but the reinstall failed.

reinstall.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English install English reinstall From re- + install.

d.g: To restore to a former position or rank.
To bring back into use or existence; resurrect.
d.x: The ancient taboo, which Plato wishes to reinstate, is an important element.

reinstate.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- Proto-Italic *status Latin statuslbor. Old French estatbor. …

d.g: To insure again (extending or replacing prior insurance).
To place insurance on the contract that insures something (allowing the insurer to offset risk in the same way the insuree did).

reinsure.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English insure English reinsure From re- + insure.

d.g: To integrate again or in a different manner.
To restore something to a state of integration.

reintegrate.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English integrate English reintegrate From re- + integrate.

d.g: To interpret again.
d.x: If you look at it that way, you can reinterpret all the old evidence so that it supports the new theory.

reinterpret.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English interpret English reinterpret From re- + interpret.

d.g: To introduce again.
d.x: Cheap mid-week return tickets were reintroduced by British Railways on May 7, to encourage holiday travel during the week rather than at weekends.

reintroduce.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English introduce English reintroduce From re- + introduce.

d.g: To invent again something that has already been invented.
To adapt into a different form; to give a new style or image to.
d.x: He had the ability to reinvent himself as needed.

reinvent.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English invent English reinvent From re- + invent.

d.g: To give new life, energy or strength to someone or something; to revitalize.

reinvigorate.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English invigorate English reinvigorate From re- + invigorate.

d.g: To say or do (something) for a second time, such as for emphasis.
d.x: Let me reiterate my opinion.

d.g: To say or do (something) repeatedly.
d.x: That with reiterated crimes he might / Heap on himself damnation.

d.g: To say (something) for a second time, but word it differently.
d.x: Was I hard to understand? Sorry, I'll try to reiterate.

d.g: Reiterated; repeated.

reiterate.e: Early 15th century, from Late Latin reiteratus, past participle of reiterare (“to repeat”) from re- (“again”) + iterare (“to repeat”) from iterum (“again”).

d.g: To rearrange or tweak (something), especially in order to improve it or make it suitable for some purpose.
d.x: They simply cannot deliver what they promised. Nor will an affronted, alienated Brussels help them do so. Rejigged single market access? Forget it.

d.g: To provide (a place, etc.) with new equipment or machinery; to reequip, to refit.
To separate or sort (ore) again in a jigger or sieve.
A rearrangement, a reorganization.

rejig.e: The verb is derived from re- (prefix meaning ‘again, anew’) + jig (“to move briskly; to move with jerks or vibrations”). The noun is derived from the verb.

d.g: To be very happy, be delighted, exult; to feel joy.
d.x: Leicester closed out the win to spark emotional scenes as those inside Wembley rejoiced in a landmark victory.

d.g: To make happy, exhilarate.
d.x: Were he [Cain] alive, it would rejoice his soul to see what mischief it had made.

rejoice.e: From Middle English rejoicen, rejoisen, from Old French resjoir. Doublet of rejoy. Compare French réjouir; Spanish regocijar; Portuguese regozijar; Italian gioire

d.g: To join again; to unite after separation.
To come, or go, again into the presence of; to join the company of again.
d.x: Meet and rejoin me, in my penſive Grott.

d.g: To answer, as the defendant to the plaintiff's replication.
To re-insert a patent claim, typically after allowance of a patent application, applied to patent claims that had been withdrawn from examination under a restriction requirement, based on rejoinder.

rejoin.e: From Middle English rejoynen, partly from Middle French rejoin- (stem of rejoindre, from re- (“again”) + joindre (“to join”)) and partly from re- + joynen. By surface analysis, re- + join. Doublet of rejoinder.

d.g: To render young again.
To give new energy or vigour to; to revitalise.
d.x: The exercise involved in recrafting the past, past encounters and memories actually rejuvenates short-term and present memory — remarkably!

rejuvenate.e: From re- (“again”) + Latin iuvenis (“young”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare Old French rejuvener. Displaced native Middle English gingen, from Old English *ġinġan (literally “to make young”), equivalent to Old English ġeong + Old English -an.

d.g: To kindle again.
To be kindled or ignited again.
To revive.
d.x: After being abroad for a decade, when he came back he rekindled his obsession with cricket.

d.g: Synonym of reflash.

rekindle.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English kindle English rekindle From re- + kindle.

d.g: To lace again.

relace.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English lace English relace From re- + lace.

d.g: To tell in a descriptive way.
d.x: The captain related an old yarn.

d.g: To be relevant specifically to.
d.x: These regulations relate only to exported goods.

d.g: To bring into a relation, association, or connection (between one thing and another).
To have a connection.
d.x: The patterns on the screen relate to the pitch and volume of the music being played.

relate.e: From Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“carry back; report”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of refer. See also infer, collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prefer and prelate among others.

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of relativize.
To make one thing relative to another.
To make relative.
d.x: to relativize indirect objects

relativize.e: English relative Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English relativize From relative + -ize.

d.g: To make something loose.
d.x: to relax a rope or cord

d.g: To relieve from constipation; to loosen; to open.
d.x: An aperient relaxes the bowels.

d.g: To become loose.
To relieve (someone or someone's mind) of stress; to enable to rest; to calm down.
d.x: Amusement relaxes the mind.

relax.e: From Middle English relaxen, from Old French relaxer, from Latin relaxāre (“relax, loosen, open”), from re- (“back”) + laxāre (“loosen”), from laxus (“loose, free”). By surface analysis, re- + lax (“open, free, loose”).

d.g: To learn (something) again.
d.x: I had to relearn how to swim properly.

relearn.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *leys- Proto-Indo-European *(le-)lóys-e Proto-Germanic *lizanąder. Proto-West Germanic *liʀnōn Old English leornian Middle English lernen English learn English relearn From re- + learn.

d.g: Exile or banish to a particular place.
Banish from proximity to Rome for a set time; compare relegate.
d.x: Eventually his freedom of speech drove Vespasian to relegate him a second time, and shortly after he was executed […].

d.g: Remove or send to a place far away.
Consign (a person or thing) to a place, position, or role of obscurity, insignificance, oblivion, lower rank or (especially) inferiority.
d.x: Her bright ideas were relegated to "tosh" by her manager.

relegate.e: First attested in 1561, borrowed from Latin relēgātus, the past participle of relēgō (“to dispatch, banish”).

d.g: A stay; a stop; a delay.
d.x: There was no relent, my dear, as we pulled each other in.

d.g: To give in or be swayed; to become less hard, harsh, or cruel; to show clemency.
d.x: He had planned to ground his son for a month, but relented and decided to give him a stern lecture instead.

d.g: To slacken; to abate.
d.x: We waited for the storm to relent before we ventured outside.

d.g: To become less rigid or hard; to soften; to yield, for example by dissolving or melting
d.x: [Salt of tartar] placed in a cellar will […] begin to relent.

relent.e: From Middle English relenten, from Anglo-Norman relentir, from Latin re- + lentare (“to bend”), from lentus (“soft, pliant, slow”). Earliest recording dates to 1526. The noun is from the verb.

d.g: To ease (a person, person's thoughts etc.) from mental distress; to stop (someone) feeling anxious or worried, to alleviate the distress of.
d.x: I was greatly relieved by the jury's verdict.

d.g: To ease (someone, a part of the body etc.) or give relief from physical pain or discomfort.
To alleviate (pain, distress, mental discomfort etc.).
To provide comfort or assistance to (someone in need, especially in poverty).

relieve.e: From Late Middle English releven, from Old French relever, specifically from the conjugated forms such as (jeo) relieve (“I lift up”), and its source, Latin relevo (“to lift up, lighten, relieve, alleviate”), combined form of re- (“back”) + levo (“to lift”). Doublet of relevate. Compare levant, levity, etc.

d.g: To add new lines to.
To add a new lining to.
A eutectic mixture of choline chloride and urea.

reline.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English line English reline From re- + line.

d.g: To give up, abandon or retire from something; to trade away.
d.x: to relinquish a title

d.g: To let go (free, away), physically release.
To metaphorically surrender, yield control or possession.
To accept to give up, withdraw etc.
d.x: The delegations saved the negotiations by relinquishing their incompatible claims to sole jurisdiction.

relinquish.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re- Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- Proto-Indo-European *-né- Proto-Indo-European *linékʷti Proto-Italic *linkʷō Latin linquō Latin relinquō Old French relenquir Middle French relinquirbor. …

d.g: To experience (something) again; to live over again.
d.x: I relive that horrible accident every night and wake screaming.

d.g: To come back to life.

relive.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *h₂en-der. Proto-Germanic *an Proto-West Germanic *ana Old English on Proto-Indo-European *leyp- Proto-Germanic *lībanąder. Proto-Germanic *lībą Proto-West Germanic *līb Old English līfder. …

d.g: To load (something) again.
d.x: If you need to reload film, the cassette can be rewound slightly by turning the hub located on one end of its spool.

d.g: To refresh a copy of a program etc. in memory or of a web page etc. on screen
To load a gun again; or recharge a used cartridge.
d.x: Naturally after firing solidly for five minutes without reloading Arnie has wiped out all the bad dudes and thumbs a lift to the nearest town.

d.g: To replay music in a DJ set.
d.x: We're gonna make the stars come out tonight. So why don't you reload,reload, re reload the music?

reload.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English load English reload From re- + load.

d.g: To move (something) from one place to another.
d.x: We had to relocate the magazine rack because we bruised our shins on it too frequently when it was near the door.

d.g: To change one's domicile or place of business.
d.x: Alfred relocated to Colorado Springs to take advantage of the boom in the defense industry.

d.g: To lose something and find it again.
d.x: I relocated the bird I spotted last week.

relocate.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English locate English relocate From re- + locate.

d.g: To trust; to have confidence in; to depend.
d.x: I relied on "George" and "Fred"—the autopilot and the flight director—to fly the airplane while I worked my way through […]

rely.e: From Middle English relien, from Old French relier (“fasten, attach, rally, oblige”), from Latin religo (“fasten, bind fast”), from re- + ligo.

d.g: write new lyrics for (a song)
That which is left; relic; remainder.
That which is left of a human being after the life is gone; relics; a dead body.
Posthumous works or productions, especially literary works.
To stay after others or other parts have been removed or otherwise disappeared.
d.x: After three rounds of interviews, only 5 candidates remained.

remain.e: From Middle English remainen, from Old French remain-, stressed stem of remanoir, from Latin remaneō, maneō, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stay”). …

d.g: To marry a second or subsequent time (the same spouse or a different one) after the end of a marriage.
d.x: After his wife's death, he never remarried.

remarry.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English marry English remarry From re- + marry.

d.g: To correct or improve (a deficiency or problem).
To recall from one's memory; to have an image in one's memory.
d.x: In the lightness of my heart I sang catches of songs as my horse gayly bore me along the well-remembered road.

d.g: To memorize; to put something into memory.
d.x: Please remember this formula!

d.g: To keep in mind; to be mindful of.
d.x: Remember what I've said.

d.g: To not forget (to do something required)
d.x: Remember to lock the door when you go out.

remember.e: From Middle English remembren, from Old French remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorari (“to remember again”), from re- + memor (“mindful”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-, *(s)mer- (“to think about, be mindful, remember”). …

d.g: Alternative form of remilitarize.
To militarize (a demilitarized area) again.
To cause one to experience a memory (of someone or something); to bring to the notice or consideration (of a person).
d.x: I am aware, reader, and you need not remind me, that it is a dreadful thing for a parson to be warlike: […]

d.g: An act of reminding; a reminder.

remind.e: From mid 17th century, equivalent to re- + mind (“to remember”). Probably suggested by obsolete rememorate with the same sense. Displaced Old English myndgian.

d.g: To recall the past in a private moment, often fondly or nostalgically.
d.x:
But in the blink of an eye, you kissed me goodbye
And I reminisced of a better time

d.g: To talk or write about memories of the past, especially pleasant memories.
To remember fondly; to reminisce about.
d.x:
And now when life begins to get the best of me
I reminisce these childhood memories

d.g: An act of reminiscence.
d.x: I met up with Alastair McQueen [former Mirror colleague] and we had a reminisce.

reminisce.e: Back-formation from reminiscence, from Latin reminīscēns, present participle of reminīscor (“to remember”).

d.g: To change the appearance, layout, or furnishings of.
d.x: Modern engine sheds of advanced design have also been built at Radyr, Abercynon, and elsewhere, whilst other depots have been remodelled and re-equipped.

d.g: Synonym of remodeling.
d.x: The work on this remodel was slow going.

remodel.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *med- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Italic *medos Late Latin modus Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Late Latin -ulus Late Latin modulusder. …

d.g: mold again, apply a new mold to

remold.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English mold English remold From re- + mold.

d.g: To object with in critical fashion; to express disapproval (with, against).
Specifically, to lodge an official objection (especially by means of a remonstrance) with a monarch or other ruling body.
d.x: In 1753-4, the Parlements of Aix, Bordeaux, Rennes and Rouen remonstrated in support of the exiled Paris institution.

d.g: To state or plead as an objection, formal protest, or expression of disapproval.
d.x: "Belinda," remonstrated Mr. Pocket, from the other end of the table, "how can you be so unreasonable? […]"

d.g: To point out; to show clearly; to make plain or manifest; hence, to prove; to demonstrate.
d.x: I might remonstrate how great, and how sure , and how persevering mercies a pious father of a family may derive upon his succeeding generations

remonstrate.e: From (the participle stem of) Late Latin remōnstrō, from Latin re- + mōnstrō.

d.g: To mould or shape again.
To reshape or redesign.
d.x: He could not change that which has remoulded itself to resist change.

remould.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English mould English remould From re- + mould.

d.g: To compensate; to pay.
d.x: The workers were generously remunerated for their time.

remunerate.e: From the participle stem of Latin remūnerō (“to reward”), from mūnus (“gift”). Unrelated to money.

d.g: To give a new name to.
d.x: Taipei County was upgraded to the status as a special municipality in 2010 and renamed New Taipei.

d.g: An instance of renaming.
d.x:
warning: detected divergent renames of foo to:
bar
quux

rename.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ Proto-Germanic *namô Proto-West Germanic *namō Old English nama Middle English name English name English rename From re- + name.

d.g: To separate into parts with force or sudden violence; to split; to burst.
d.x: Powder rends a rock in blasting.

d.g: To violently disturb the peace of; to throw into chaos.
d.x: a scream that rent the air

d.g: To part or tear off forcibly; to take away by force; to amputate.
d.x: A time to rent, and a time to sow: a time to keepe silence, and a time to speake.

d.g: To be rent or torn; to become parted; to separate; to split.
d.x: Relationships may rend if tempers flare.

rend.e: From Middle English renden, from Old English rendan (“to rend, tear, cut, lacerate, cut down”), from Proto-West Germanic *(h)randijan (“to tear”), of uncertain origin. …

d.g: negociate anew
To negotiate new terms to replace old ones.

renegotiate.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English negotiate English renegotiate From re- + negotiate.

d.g: To make (something) new again; to restore to freshness or original condition.
d.x:
In such a night
 Medea gather’d the enchanted herbs
 That did renew old Æson.

d.g: To replace (something which has broken etc.); to replenish (something which has been exhausted), to keep up a required supply of.
To make new spiritually; to regenerate.
d.x: For which cause we faint not, but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.

d.g: To begin again; to recommence.
d.x: This murder has been a cold case for decades until last year when the new sheriff renewed the investigation.

renew.e: From Middle English renewen, an alteration (possibly on analogy with Latin renovāre) of earlier anewen (“to renew”), from Old English nīewian (“to restore; renovate; renew”), equivalent to re- + new. …

d.g: Alternative spelling of renormalize.

renormalise.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English normalise English renormalise From re- + normalise.

d.g: To subject to renormalization
To make the norm again.

renormalize.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Latin norma Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-der.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālis Latin nōrmālisder. …

d.g: An act of renouncing.
To give up, resign, surrender.
d.x: to renounce a title to land or to a throne

d.g: To cast off, repudiate.
d.x:
This world I do renounce, and in your sights
Shake patiently my great affliction off.

d.g: To decline further association with someone or something, disown.

renounce.e: From Old French renoncier (French renoncer), from Latin renūntiō. Doublet of renunciate.

d.g: To renew; to revamp something to make it look new again.
d.x: This house is shabby: it needs renovating.

d.g: To restore to freshness or vigor.

renovate.e: The adjective first attested in 1440, the verb in 1535; from Middle English renovat(e) (“renewed”), from Latin renovātus, perfect passive participle of renovō (“to renew”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

d.g: To open (something) again.
d.x: Says Barnes: "The next priority [for Devon County Council] is reopening the line from Tavistock to Plymouth.

d.g: To open again.
d.x: Yet city officials said unburned sections of the upscale Westfield Galleria at Roseville could reopen within weeks, in time for the holiday shopping season.

reopen.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *upó Proto-Germanic *ub Proto-Germanic *upp Proto-Germanic *upanaz Proto-West Germanic *opan Old English open Middle English open English open English reopen From re- + open.

d.g: Alternative spelling of reorganize.
to organize something again, or in a different manner
to undergo a reorganization

reorganize.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *werǵ-der. Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon)bor. Latin organum Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. …

d.g: To orient again; to make or become oriented after dislocation or disorientation.

reorient.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English orient English reorient From re- + orient.

d.g: To orientate anew; to cause to face a different direction.
To paint anew or again, especially if recently painted.
d.x: to repaint a house; to repaint the ground of a picture

d.g: To draw or render again on the display.
d.x: To force a window to repaint itself programmatically, you call the inherited Invalidate() method[…]

d.g: The act or process of painting something again, especially if recently painted.
d.x: They didn't like the color so we had to do a repaint.

d.g: The act of drawing or rendering again on the display.

repaint.e: Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English paint English repaint From re- + paint (“verb”).

d.g: Synonym of pay back in all senses.
d.x: I finally repaid my student loans, just before sending my kids to college.

d.g: To make worthwhile; to yield a result worth the effort; to pay off.
d.x: The possible importance of excessive androgen secretion and the ingestion of agents such as the fluorenamines may repay further investigation.

d.g: To give in return; requite.
To pay (cover with tar, pitch, etc.) again.

repay.e: From Old French repaier (“to pay back”), from re- + paiier (“to pay”), from Latin pācāre (“to settle, to make peaceful”), from pāx (“peace”) + -ō (forming verbs). Equivalent to re- + pay. Cognate with repacify and French repayer (“to pay again”).

d.g: To reject, put off (a request, demand etc.).
To ward off (a malignant influence, attack etc.).
To drive back (an assailant, advancing force etc.).
d.x: In nearby Zintan, rebels repelled an advance by Gaddafi's forces, killing eight and taking one prisoner, a local activist said.

d.g: To force away by means of a repulsive force.

repel.e: From Middle English repellen, a borrowing from Old French *repeller, from Latin repellere (“to drive back”), from re- (“back”) + pellere (“to drive”). Doublet of repeal.

d.g: To feel pain, sorrow, or regret for what one has done or omitted to do; the cause for repenting may be indicated with "of".
d.x: Marry in haste, repent at leisure.

d.g: To be sorry for sin as morally evil, and to seek forgiveness; to cease to practice sin and to love.
d.x: I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.

d.g: To feel pain on account of; to remember with sorrow.
d.x: If Aljunied decides to go that way (to vote for the Workers' Party), well Aljunied has five years to live and repent.

d.g: To be sorry for, to regret.

d.g: To consider (a function) as defined on a subset of its original domain.

restrict.e: Borrowed from Latin restrictus, perfect passive participle of restringō (“draw back tightly; restrain, restrict”), from re- (“back, again”) + stringō (“press, tighten, compress”). Doublet of ristretto as an adjective.

d.g: To change the organization of.
To modify the terms of a loan, providing relief to a debtor who would otherwise be forced to default.
A reorganization.

d.g: To sublime again.

d.g: To come once again to the surface.

d.g: To surface again; to reappear or re-occur.

d.g: To restore consciousness, vigor, or life to.

d.g: To regain consciousness.

d.g: To suspend again.
To undergo (or cause to undergo) resuspension.

d.g: To prepare (flax, hemp etc.) for further processing by soaking, which facilitates separation of fibers from the woody parts of the stem.

d.g: Abbreviation of retired.
Clipping of reiteration.

retaliate.e: From Latin retāliātus, past participle of retāliō (“to requite, retaliate”).

d.g: To cease use or production of something.
